segments.title: A DRAWER IN THE DESIGN
notes: Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions
segments.angle: What is the fundamental problem or need that this note/idea is trying to address? Is it addressing a symptom or the root cause? (Think: Five Whys)

sources.text: Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions: Don't live your life by default. Live your life by design.
Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions: It does more for your self-belief to say you'll meditate for 10 minutes and actually do 10 minutes vs saying you'll do 30 minutes and only doing 20 minutes.
Reality Transurfing: Whatever thoughts you send out into the world will return to you like a boomerang.

Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions: Every action you take should be intentional and deliberately thought out. Each and every decision you make should have a purpose that brings you closer to your goals.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You've stood in a kitchen late at night. The house has gone quiet. And you've noticed most of your week got decided by whatever came through the door.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The note starts right there. I'll read it exactly: Don't live your life by default. Live your life by design.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ah, the design! Most people hear that and picture a grand plan drawn up in advance, every road marked on the map, and then the living is only marching to a drum. Draft the plan first, obey it after, and the empire holds. That is the common belief, and I hold it with my whole chest.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So a design is a list you write first and then follow.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Precisely.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Hold on to that. I think it's the bit that breaks.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The note's real claim is less grand than a map and more binding than any map ever was.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Go on, then.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A design lives or dies in the keeping. It shows you how with a small case: It does more for your self-belief to say you'll meditate for 10 minutes and actually do 10 minutes vs saying you'll do 30 minutes and only doing 20 minutes.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The grandest part I hold in reserve until you have tested it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So you're saying the plan only counts once you actually keep it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Real, and binding, March. A promise made to oneself is the only contract nobody can wriggle out of, because nobody else holds the pen.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then test it on me. This week I'm writing my own version. Line one.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Walk for 10 minutes after the kettle goes off. I tick it when I'm back at the door.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A walk? Ten minutes is a rounding error, March.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A design must be large enough to hold a life, or it is only a shopping list pinned to a fridge.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It holds a stroll. That's plenty for a Thursday.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Next line. I said I'd do 30 minutes on Sunday and I did 20.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the rule is that what I write is what I do. And I write the 10.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Oh, the indignity! Listen to her. The lady has broken a vow to a walk and calls it a rule. Such a grand little confession.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ouch, fair.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A design, March, is a vow made in the first person. Only a mind quite sure of itself keeps one.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Vows are for weddings. I'm not marrying a walk.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Last line I'm writing in pencil. So faint you can't read it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That one stays in the drawer.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A drawer! Good heavens, March, now the house has a hidden room. A locket, a letter to the chair, a promise to become a lighthouse keeper, or the grandest thing of all, a crown tucked behind the teacups.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Whatever it is, I cannot wait to guess.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And since we are rummaging, J deserves a new title: Grand Architect of the Early Hours, fit for a person who builds before the kettle boils.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nope. Architects wear slippers and forget the milk.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And here's the thing about your guesses. Every one has a crown in it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's your default, not mine. It's the very thing the note warns about when it talks about living by default.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the mirror is in the room too, March. The note says: Whatever thoughts you send out into the world will return to you like a boomerang.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So a design written from a hidden state drifts toward whatever that state is sending out.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Which means the writing down isn't the root. Ask why it got skipped, then why that.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The note stops at the page. The mirror keeps going.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ask why over and over, as the old workmen did, and a grey morning turns up at the bottom of every skipped line.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: For someone who believes this, the list is short. Each morning you check it against one question: do this morning's choices still point the same way?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A missed walk is a course correction, not a verdict. For someone who doesn't believe it, the list hangs on the wall like a notice. The days get decided by the kettle, the door, and whatever the mirror happens to show.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The kettle again. Very well, the kettle has the last word on every grey morning.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So I shall end where the note began, in that late kitchen...

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: ...which you're now calling the first house blueprint of your grand empire, drawn on the back of an envelope.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The only design that counts is the one you keep on a Tuesday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the drawer, March? I shall guess it in my sleep.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Don't.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I shall dream it instead, and the dream will have a crown in it.

segments.title: THE BENT MORNING AND THE MIRROR'S RETURN
notes: Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions
segments.angle: How was this problem (or a similar one) addressed in the past (e.g., 10, 50, 100 years ago)? What can be learned from previous attempts or contexts?

sources.text: Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions: Don't live your life by default. Live your life by design.
Be Intentional With Your Life and Actions: It does more for your self-belief to say you'll meditate for 10 minutes and actually do 10 minutes vs saying you'll do 30 minutes and only doing 20 minutes.
Reality Transurfing: Whatever thoughts you send out into the world will return to you like a boomerang.
Reality Transurfing: The world is a mirror.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You've got a list pinned up somewhere. Sunday evening, you look at it, and the week slides past it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ah, the sea wall! Most people think a design is a plan drawn in advance, every road marked, and then living is only marching between the marks. Draw it first, obey it after. That is the belief, and I hold it steadily.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the plan comes first, and the day has to fit it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Exactly. The list is the blueprint. The week is the builder's obedience.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right. Not buying the sea wall.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The tide doesn't care about the paint.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The note's real claim goes deeper than any plan, and it lives in the mirror. Hear its words: Whatever thoughts you send out into the world will return to you like a boomerang.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So a plan you keep is a thought sent out, and it comes back as a day that matches it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Precisely. A plan broken is a crooked thought, and a crooked thought returns as a crooked morning.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Show me. Use the note's own example.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Gladly. The note says: It does more for your self-belief to say you'll meditate for 10 minutes and actually do 10 minutes vs saying you'll do 30 minutes and only doing 20 minutes.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine. Morning one: I write 10 minutes, I sit 10 minutes, the timer face down on the cushion. Another morning I write 30, stop at 20, and the timer's still ticking on the counter.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The first is a kept word. The other is a word bent to fit the day.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And here is the hard part, and I will not soften it. The bent morning is the one that feels like yours. You remember the stretch and forget the promise...

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: ...The mirror learns from the bend. Brutal. And I did do 20, and I felt okay about it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Fine! The most dangerous word in any house.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Don't crown it. Fine is just fine.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Oh, the poor grid.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Long ago, young Benjamin Franklin kept a little book with a grid of virtues, one row for each, and a small black mark for every fault he caught in himself each day.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Tidy man.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He confessed that order was the hardest of them, and he kept the grid anyway.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He failed at order and kept the chart. That's the useful bit.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The chart was a standing conversation between a man and his own pen.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Pen's the wrong word. It was a chart, and charts don't crown anyone. Back to the grid. What does it show that the mirror doesn't?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That the marks were seen. A mark is a message, March, and the mirror sends it back.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So here's where they cross. The design note says every decision points one way. The reality note says what you send out comes back. Put them together, and a broken entry isn't only a missed task.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's a signal that returns as a day that feels decided by the kettle and the door.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The kettle again. You are never without it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The kettle's mine. I'm not giving it up.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I shall guess the drawer. A tally of every time you were wrong, perhaps, tied up in ribbon and topped with a crown.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nope. Still guessing crowns.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's your default, not the note's.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A morning with the grid is a short talk with yourself, one question asked before the coffee cools: do today's choices still point where I wrote them? A missed entry is a nudge, and you go back to the page.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Someone who waves the idea off reads that same page as a verdict. Every empty box is proof the day was never theirs to begin with.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A hard truth, March, since you handed me the pen. Most grids on most walls are never read after the first week. The paper does nothing.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Harsh. Also true. Which is why the reading is the job.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Back to the Sunday and the sea wall. The tide doesn't care about the paint.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The person standing on it decides whether to keep walking.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the crown is mine, the kettle keeps its vote, and I concede... that a design kept on a Tuesday is the only one that counts.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Thank you. Up next, Happiness And Gratitude and When You're Scared To Take Action.

segments.title: THE CARD BY THE TIME CLOCK
notes: When You're Scared To Take Action
segments.angle: What are the potential ethical implications or societal consequences (positive or negative) of this idea if widely adopted? How could it be misused?

sources.text: Happiness And Gratitude: When you smile, your brain automatically assumes you're having a good time.
Happiness And Gratitude: Happiness is not something that is earned or deserved.
Happiness And Gratitude: Happiness is simply a state of mind in which our thinking is pleasant most of the time.
Happiness And Gratitude: The more grateful you are for something, the more doing it will release dopamine.
When You're Scared To Take Action: Bravery is earned, not granted.
When You're Scared To Take Action: Fear is resolved through action. You can't think it away.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Somebody tells you to smile through a bad morning. So you do, and the smile sits in your chest like a cold coin. You feel worse than before. Then you wonder if you just lied to your own brain.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ah, the poor smile, pressed into service like a footman at a funeral! Let me give you the belief most people hold. A feeling must be earned before it is allowed. You may be cheerful once you have deserved it, and not one minute sooner. Cheer is a wage, paid on merit.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Deserve it first, then feel it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Sounds fair, the way a bouncer sounds fair. Nobody lets themselves laugh until they've checked their paperwork.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Charming, March, and quite wrong, which is my favourite kind of wrong. The note says it plainly: Happiness is simply a state of mind in which our thinking is pleasant most of the time. No wage. No merit. No ledger at the door.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ouch. Fair.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So happiness is the weather in your head.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It isn't a prize you go out and win.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The weather, yes, and weather simply arrives. The note goes further. Happiness is not a moral issue, any more than the circulation of blood is one. You do not earn a pulse.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You don't earn a pulse. Nice. But it still sounds like something printed on a poster. Show me the weather in an actual room.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Gladly. But the note's real claim lies beneath the weather, and I shall hold it back until we reach the room where it can breathe. You will want it when you hear it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I want it now. Hold it back and I'll sulk.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Give me the room.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Imagine a laminated card zip-tied beside the time clock in a warehouse break room. It reads: Gratitude releases dopamine. Beneath it hangs a sign-in sheet, and the people reading it have just heard that the extra hours are gone. They are asked to write a few things they are thankful for before the shift begins, and then they walk out onto the floor.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Oof. Thankful for the dock door and the hum of the strip lights. Then straight onto the line with the worry still in their pockets.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The card looks cheerful. The room is not. He'd hate that card, by the way, and so would I.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A leash with a smile painted on it, March. The poster says the chemical follows the thankfulness, so the thankfulness becomes the duty, and the duty becomes the proof that the worker is doing the job well.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ha. Painted leash.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Hold on. The card says gratitude makes you feel good. The sheet says gratitude is the job.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Only one of those is on the timesheet.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Quite right, my lady with teeth. And the gap between the poster and the sheet is exactly where the harm lives.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Harm's a big word. Pick a smaller one.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then call it a nudge. A soft push, with a smile on the handle.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nudge. Okay. Who gets blamed when the nudge doesn't work?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The worker, of course.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Naturally. Downhill, as always.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The poster says gratitude releases dopamine, so a worker who still feels flat reads their own gloom as a failure to be thankful enough. The fault moves from the sheet to the person holding the pen. A clever trick, and an ugly one.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's one to me. You're down a point.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I'm keeping count.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You keep a ledger, March?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Everyone has a ledger. Mine just has a kettle on it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then here is another room, a call centre's training binder. Its first rule: smile before you pick up the line, because the caller can hear a frown down the wire. I name you, J, Keeper of the Night Bell, for whoever keeps such binders in the small hours of the mind.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Night Bell. No.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's still a crown with a ringer on it. And the bell in that binder rings too often, which is a comeback I'm saving for later.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Save it, then. I shall wait by the bell. What does the binder show?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A smile trained before the call teaches the agent to read their own exhaustion as their own failure.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The caller is only a voice in a headset. The agent is the one who fails the smile. Same card, same sheet, different desk.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Hush a moment. A worker who is tired, and told to be glad, does not stop being tired. They learn only to be ashamed of the tiredness. Let that sit on the table for a while, March, because it is the slow truth of the whole business.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Sitting.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Now the crossing. Our fear note says bravery is earned, not granted. You do the thing scared and come out braver. The happiness note says feelings need no reason. Both refuse to make you clear the feeling before you move.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So the feeling may follow the act, and the act may go first. A lovely freedom. But a freedom is a key, March, and keys can be handed to others.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Yes. Somebody who controls the act can tell you to feel grateful, and tell you to act while scared. The freedom turns into the push.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Whoever holds the schedule holds the leap.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The old knife in the old drawer. Fear is resolved through action, the note says, and an employer may decide which action, and when, and leave the frightened person to believe the failure is theirs.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Give me the Tuesday, not the drawer.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Someone who believes this writes a list of gratitudes at breakfast, then walks into a frightening meeting. They step scared, once and then again, and the confidence arrives late, one shaky step at a time. Nobody checks whether the step is safe. Nobody asks whether they were sent there for someone else's gain. They just keep stepping, and they call it courage, and they go home wondering why it feels like losing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the list is no shield. A smile or a list cannot stand in for a pay slip, or a locked exit. Those are real things, and a card beside a time clock cannot repair them. I say this plainly, and I leave it plain.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Yes. Thank you. Kettle's mine, by the way.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The kettle, yes. And the first lie of the whole business was the smile from your cold open. The note never told that lie. Those who hung the notice told it, and the smile was only the costume.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Smile before the call. Smile before the shift.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay. Up next, the other half of tonight's pair: the smile note and the fear note.

segments.title: THE WHISTLE DEADLINE AND THE HARBOUR WALL
notes: When You're Scared To Take Action
segments.angle: How might I solve this in a completely unconventional or exaggerated way?

sources.text: When You're Scared To Take Action: Fear is resolved through action. You can't think it away.
When You're Scared To Take Action: But fear can only be conquered through action, not more planning.
When You're Scared To Take Action: But if you let that stop you, you will never sail past the safety of the harbour.
Happiness And Gratitude: If you wait until you "deserve" to think pleasant thoughts, you're likely to think unpleasant thoughts regarding your own unworthiness.
When You're Scared To Take Action: Bravery is earned, not granted.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You've drafted the same opening line again. Each new version feels safer than hitting send, so you save it once more and tell yourself you're preparing.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Planning's the responsible cure. Nobody walks into a fear without a map. You plan till it shrinks to a size you can step over, then you go. That's just being careful, isn't it?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Careful! What a lovely word for a parlour with the curtains drawn. Tell me, March, does the fear actually shrink while you plan it? Or does the planning lay out a warm bed for it and bring it tea?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It shrinks.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Usually by the time the draft's been reread enough to bore it to sleep.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the fear is a tame pet, fed on drafts, and you are its devoted keeper. The note will not sign off on your keeping. It is blunt, and I adore it for being blunt. Fear is resolved through action. You can't think it away.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So I can't plan my way out of being scared.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I am saying the planner who waits for the fear to leave will sit in the harbour until the hull rots. Action is the only thing that moves fear at all, March. Thinking has never carried a boat out of port, no matter how well it was drawn on the chart.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Simple, then. Plan less, do more.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Simple truths are the best truths, March. This one is plain as a coil of rope.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Oh, here we go.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Don't you call it simple. That word is what people say right before a shift goes sideways.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then call it complicated, if the word offends you. You prefer people to truths, so give me a person, and I shall give you one with a draft in her hand.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Yes. A person with a draft, and the poetry kept in your pocket.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A woman has rewritten one resignation email for years. Each night she tightens a clause, softens a sentence, saves it again, always meaning to send it tomorrow.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Sounds like most Sunday nights.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So my remedy is extravagant, as remedies ought to be: she must press send before the kettle comes to the boil. And the kettle, March, shall be the one on your counter.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Mine?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You're timing a resignation on my kettle? Kettle's mine. I said so.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Your whistle, then, your deadline. A whistle is a deadline with a face on it, and every decent kettle has one.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A whistle means tea. Nobody's ever resigned because the water got hot.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Nobody resigns properly while they wait, March. They stand at the edge of the sentence, and the waiting becomes the deadline that never comes.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And what if the email has a typo? Send it, and the typo stays sent forever.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the typo will survive, and so will she. Perfection was never on the kettle's list. Sending is, and sending is the one part of the business fear cannot touch.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Typos sting, narrator.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And if she sends it and hates it?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then she has learned what no draft ever taught her, that the thing she dreaded was survivable. Bravery gets earned by pressing send, not by polishing the sentence for another month.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay. But why do you sound so pleased with yourself?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Because I have been sitting on the cupboard door all evening, March, and I should like your chair for the rest of the scene. Move over. I shall conduct the kettle from there.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nice try. Those grand images are the cupboard door again. Stay on the stool.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: What did you hide in this design, March? A drawer with the real answer folded inside, I suspect. You always did keep the best cups on the top shelf, and the good answer behind them.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nothing's hidden.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You're guessing, and you're guessing loudly.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Guilty as charged.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I shall guess a little longer. I have one more thing, the best part of all, and I am keeping it back until the whistle. Meanwhile, consider the harbour wall.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Have you looked at one properly? Those stones are laid to shelter boats meant to sail out. The wall takes the weather so the hull doesn't have to. Every harbour wall is a promise that the boat will go...

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Harbour walls, narrator? We're talking about a draft in a folder.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The note talks about the harbour too. But if you let that stop you, you will never sail past the safety of the harbour.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine, that's a good line. Now back to the email.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A harbour that is only admired is a waiting room with water in it, March. That is precisely where the planner lives, sails folded like napkins, the bay very pretty from the window.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Wait. That's the thing. The happiness note says you don't have to deserve the good feeling first. If you wait until you "deserve" to think pleasant thoughts, you're likely to think unpleasant thoughts about your own unworthiness.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So waiting for the feeling and waiting for bravery are the same waiting.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Exactly, and that shared waiting keeps the planner in the harbour. Both notes cut the feeling loose from its precondition, and then the planner sits on the quay waiting for a permission nobody will ever issue.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the draft stays in the folder, and the email goes out with a typo somewhere in it. They stop checking whether it's perfect, the way a swimmer stops testing the water before the jump.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: They go in cold, and they come up knowing the water held them.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And I promised you the best part, March. The polishing is the room fear lives in. Every edit is a small permission slip to wait one more night, and the note asks you to tear the slip up.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine. You're right.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Now the kettle's boiling, so I'm changing the subject. Who's making the tea?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The draft goes out before the whistle, March, and the note has the last word, as notes always do.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's the small hours, so keep the tea hot. Up next, Staying On Your Purpose.

segments.title: A DRYER'S TURN AND THE HOUR IN PIECES
segments.angle: What if this problem existed in an entirely different industry?

sources.text: Staying On Your Purpose: Spend at least 1 hour a day doing what you feel you're meant to do, now.
Staying On Your Purpose: Don't wait any longer. Don't believe the myth that "one day, things will be different". They won't.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You're at the far end of a laundrette at gone midnight. The dryers are turning under the strip lights. By the time clock there's a laminated card. Start Your Real Work Before Your Shift Ends. You read it on the way in and on the way out. It's been up there longer than you have.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Waiting's the sensible part, March. A sailor doesn't sail before he knows the coast. Find the purpose, feel sure of it, then begin. The card's just asking a man to be ready.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ready's fine. Ready's what I do while the washer's still going.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then you agree the card is kind.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I agree it's a card. Go on, then. What's the note say?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The note's not kind about waiting, and it doesn't pretend to be. Here's the claim, full size. Spend at least 1 hour a day doing what you feel you're meant to do, now. Now, March. Not after the feeling turns up. Not when the hour's convenient. I'm keeping the best bit back for later, so be patient.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So an hour a day. Doing the thing. Before I feel anything about it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you feel anything at all. The feeling follows the hour, March. It doesn't arrive first and invite the hour to tag along behind it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nice picture. But the feeling's the bit I wanted.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The feeling is the bit you're waiting for. And waiting is the only bit you're doing well.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ouch. And there's the other line. Don't believe the myth that "one day, things will be different". They won't. That's cold, narrator.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Cold, yes. But a cold bath is still a bath, March. It wakes you faster than a warm excuse, and the note knows it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right. Then let's try it on me. A week. Out loud. A night worker in a laundrette. No plan, just the hour.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Splendid. A woman at the dryers, a pencil behind her ear, and a whole night waiting to be spent. Do go on.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Monday. First hour gets squeezed between the dryer buzz and the fold stack. I write one line, buzzer goes, I stand up, I sit down. The time's in pieces.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Pieces! Pieces are how great buildings get raised, March. You're not losing the hour. You're laying it stone by stone among the sheets.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Pieces, sure. Stone by stone, next to a fold stack. Okay. Tuesday. Found a library leaflet under the change tray. Bookbinding, free classes. I want to learn it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A leaflet under the change tray! That's a sign, March. The universe slid it in with the coins. You must sew your first book. And you must sew it with dryer lint.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Lint. Dryer lint.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Fluff's the fibre of every hour that was spun and dropped on the floor. Gather it, twist it, stitch the first signature with it, so the book remembers where it came from.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A lint-stitched book's a fire hazard, narrator. There's a fire notice on that door already, and I'm reading it again.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Listen to you. A fire hazard, in a cathedral. The laundrette is a cathedral of spinning hours. Each machine is a candle that never goes out.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Candles now. Fire hazard.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Hush, the pews are listening. The benches are pews where folded sheets wait to be blessed. The buzzer is the bell, calling the faithful to their duty. And the faithful is one tired woman with a pencil behind her ear, tucking a leaflet under her thumb like a psalm. The psalm is the fluff, and the fluff is the...

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: There's the cupboard door again, swinging open. Narrator, the faithful are on their feet. Stop.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Oh, cut me off, do. The cathedral will keep its silence. Its candles too. And its fluff.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Thank you. Back to the hour. Say I'm stuck in the gap. Buzzer, fold stack, elbows deep, and the hour's gone.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the hour was never gone, March. Think of a dryer. It gets its turn on the schedule whether the load's finished or not. Your hour's a turn like that. It comes up in the gaps. It doesn't wait for the sheets to finish their argument.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So it's a turn on the schedule. Like the dryer. I don't wait for the load to finish.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Precisely, and you've said it better than I could. A dryer's never asked if the load is ready. It just gets its turn. And the gaps in the night stop being empty.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right, right. He's right, mostly.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Did you hear that? A few words and a whole admission. I shall have it engraved on the time clock.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Don't. Get off my folding table, you're leaning on my stack. The sheets are going damp.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I am sitting on the table in a state of grace, March. And since you've joined the lint business, I should like your stool for the rest of the night.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Stool stays. Chair stays. You're on the table.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then let me offer J something grander for the small hours. Lord of the Filter Screen. A man who guards the trap with his life.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's a title for the repair man who turns up with a torch. Same as the bell. Loud, and it means nothing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then you keep the grand titles, and I keep the fluff.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Score's level now. Even again. I keep my own tally, and it's tight.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then we go into the rest of the night level, and the dryers keep their own counsel.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right. The card. I've walked past it all night and never read it out loud. Shall I?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You've read it silently every shift, March. Out loud, it might stop feeling like a shrug.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Start Your Real Work Before Your Shift Ends.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: There. The card says what the note says, only in a smaller font. The real work starts now, inside the hour. And the shift ends long after the dryers stop turning.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the card was right. The whole time.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The card's the one who was right, March. And it never once needed to be grand about it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Up next, List Of Nice Things To Do. After that, The Influence Of Others, which he insists is the real reason the dryers are so loud.

segments.title: A DOOR HELD OPEN AND WHO GETS IN
notes: List Of Nice Things To Do
segments.angle: How would I explain this idea if I had to tell it like a children's fairy tale?

sources.text: The Influence Of Others: Who you allow to influence you will determine where you'll end up.
The Influence Of Others: “You are the average of the five people you spend the most time with”.
List Of Nice Things To Do: On each cutout write something that is special about your lover or a good friend.
List Of Nice Things To Do: Thank someone.
List Of Nice Things To Do: Hold the door open for someone.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's the small hours, and you're holding a door open for a woman with a basket on her hip. She says thank you as if you've handed her something real. For the length of that door, you're the nicest person on the street.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The door was never sticking, March. It was only waiting, the way the best doors wait.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And everybody knows you are the average of the five people you can point to. Count them off, and there you stand, a sum handed down by nature, the five chosen for you before you could walk.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's been sticking all night, narrator.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And the five-people line is a law you've made up. I've got a comeback for it, but I'm saving it. Nobody counts anyone in that note. It asks who you let in.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Hear it whole, March. “Who you allow to influence you will determine where you'll end up.” Your company is the hand on the tiller, and the sea does the rest.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The best bit, the part about where you end up, I'm keeping back until the wind turns. So be patient.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So who gets in decides where I finish.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right. Show me on a Tuesday, not on a ship.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Precisely, and smaller than I could ever say it. Who gets in steers the boat.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then the case. The other note's on that list too, paper hearts with something special written on each. Let's try it on me.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Sunday, kitchen counter, a stack of hearts. I write names. A mate who hums through his break. A neighbour who says thank you at the bin.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then each morning you pull one out and send that person a line about the thing you wrote.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Every morning. Fine.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A month of that, March, and you'll catch yourself humming on your own break.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You never counted the company. You chose where your attention went, and the company followed it, the way weather follows wind.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Weather, now.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Once upon a time, a woodcutter's daughter kept a box of hearts for a village that never once said thank you. Every morning she wrote one more, and the village slept easier, though it never knew why.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Why's it in a tin, though?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Why not a heap on the counter?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A box has a lid, March, and a lid says stop. It's small enough to count, so the writing gets finished, and then the hearts stop being decoration and turn into a habit. The box is the rule, and the rule is the...

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the box is the rule. Not the hearts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Quite so. Every rule is a cupboard door, swinging open on its own...

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Cupboard door's swung open again. Let it swing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Very well. The cupboard has the last word, and it's a draughty one.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Back to the line. Influence.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The lid is the count, and the count is who I choose. Five names, a month, a habit. That's the tangent paying off. It was the count that mattered, not the hearts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The count is the company, March. Five names, finished, become the company that finishes you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Which is the note's whole argument, dressed in glitter.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: But the other note isn't only about getting. Thank someone. That's on the list, and nice things go out into the world.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Thank someone is exactly where the notes cross, March. Every thank you hands a little of you out, and every person thanked hands a little back.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You are choosing who gets to shape you, and whom you shape in turn. Giving is a door too, and it opens both ways.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So giving is letting in.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The influence note turned round.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Precisely. One note says be generous, the other says be choosy, and neither shows the whole of it alone.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Together they say you are the average of who you let in and of who you give to. And for J, for the small hours, a new title: Keeper of the Open Door.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's a title for the bloke who fixes the door closer.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Loud, and it'll stick.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fork, short. Someone who believes this keeps a box of paper cutouts by the front door. Every morning the hand lands on a name chosen on purpose. There's no crowd in it. There's one quiet choice repeated, until the company looks like the company they wanted.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the door is only a door, March.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's kind, if you hold it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The thank you was the whole point.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Agreed, the stranger's thank you was the real thing, and I'll concede it in writing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I shall take your chair for the close, March, since a kind man ought to sit once he's agreed.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Chair stays.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Here's the comeback I saved. Five people don't make you, narrator. They only tell you who stopped to say thank you.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I'm holding this one open with my foot, and the card by the time clock would have said all of this shorter. I was right.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Up next, Your Self Identity, Beliefs Dictate How You Live. Bring a box.

segments.title: THE LID THAT MAKES A COMPANY
notes: List Of Nice Things To Do
segments.angle: What if I had limitless resources or time to solve this?

sources.text: The Influence Of Others: “You are the average of the five people you spend the most time with”. Who you allow to influence you will determine where you'll end up.
The Influence Of Others: Only surround yourself with people who will better your life and pull you higher. Cut out all who drag you down or hinder your growth.
List Of Nice Things To Do: Gift Idea: Put 50–100 paper hearts or smiley faces in a box. On each cutout write something that is special about your lover or a good friend.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You're standing at the sink after a long shift, and a friend says the people you sit with are the people you'll become. You feel the small drop in your stomach as you count them off, checking whether you like the answer.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A fixed sum, March. Five seats at the table, handed out before you could walk, and nobody gets a vote on the seating plan. You don't choose the count. You read it off like a tide table.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So whoever's at my table is the whole deal. That's the bit I'm supposed to swallow?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Swallow it, and the current does the work. Nature keeps the ledger, March, and you are its entry.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Not a ledger. The note says who you let in. Nobody's counting anyone.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Hear it whole, then. “Only surround yourself with people who will better your life and pull you higher.” That is a sentence about choosing, and choosing is the hard part of the whole business.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Noted, narrator.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine, choosing. Then test it. Say I've got limitless time and limitless everything. A bottomless tin of hearts, a whole list of names, and a Sunday that never ends. Which name goes in first?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The one who has been kindest to you, March, the one you owe the sum to. Put that heart at the centre of the table and let every other name gather round it like iron filings.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's a feeling. Not a reason. Why that one?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Because the first heart is the first vote. Every name after it is a vote for the same sort of company.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right. But if the tin's bottomless, I write everyone. Every name I've ever met. So why does the box still have a lid?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ah. Now you ask the question a king would never think to ask, so the answer belongs to the throne. Imagine a kingdom of hearts, March. Heralds with baskets. Every road lined with a heart, every bench, every bell rope, a whole realm kind to itself by decree, signed in gold.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Cut it down. One counter, one biro, one Tuesday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: But the kingdom is the vision...

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Kingdom's out. Counter's in. Tuesday. Write down one person.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Very well. A kingdom reduced to a kitchen counter. I'm wounded, and also being made to hold a biro.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Hold it. Write.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: There was once a king who owned every hour in the realm and every loaf in the granary.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Every loaf?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He sat at every feast in his kingdom, and he sat at them all alone, because nothing was ever refused him, so nothing was ever chosen for him either.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the king's the proof.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The king is the proof. Infinite hours, infinite hearts, and an empty feast. Nobody had to be picked, so nobody was particular.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Hang on. The king had no lid. No limit, so no choosing, so his feast was just a crowd. A crowd that's never been picked.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A crowd is worse than an empty chair, March. The chair at least knows it's waiting.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ouch.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the lid is what makes it a company. The box only holds so many, so every person in it is a choice. Take the lid off and anybody walks in, and nobody has been picked. The lid was the whole point.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The lid wins.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now then. J needs a new title, and I have one ready. Warden of the Open Tin.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Better. It still sounds like a bloke with a biscuit tin.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Here is where the notes meet, March. The gift note asks you to give freely. The influence note asks you to choose carefully. Give to anyone and the giving spreads thin. Choose and never give, and the choosing becomes a locked room.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fair enough, narrator.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the limitless test shows both at once. I can give to everybody, which means the real question is who goes in the box. Generosity with no circle spreads thin, and choice with no giving is a closed door. Neither note shows that alone.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Quite. Unlimited time shows what neither note shows alone. The giving needs the circle, and the circle needs the giving, or it's just a club with a lock on it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A club with a lock on it. Got it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Someone who believes this has a tin on the windowsill. Each morning they draw one card and send one line. The tin never gets bigger than they can fill on purpose, and it never stays empty for long. Give it a while, and the company starts to look like the company they picked.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the bottomless tin, March, the one with no lid?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then it's never empty, and I still pick what goes in it. Also, I've built a bit into my own design that's only mine. I'm not saying what.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A drawer, I'd wager. Keep it shut, then, the way the best drawers keep.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Back to the door, narrator. Say a woman with a basket thanks you as if you'd handed her something real. Would you know what to do with that thank you?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The door never stuck, March. The lady with the basket simply knew how to wait for it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You've been holding it open yourself, narrator. Stop pretending it's the door.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And Keeper of the Open Door still belongs to the chap who oils the hinge. Warden I'll give you. Tally's tight, by the way.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I am to sit on a stool, and a stool, March, is an insult to a storyteller's dignity. Mind you, it's a very sturdy stool, and I shall say no more about it. Complaint noted.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Up next, Focus On One Thing (No Shiny Object Syndrome), then Embodiment, Be Who You Strive To Be. Bring a tin.

segments.title: THE MOUNTAIN WITH A MAST ON IT
notes: Focus On One Thing (No Shiny Object Syndrome)
Embodiment - Be Who You Strive To Be
segments.angle: What would happen if this idea were merged with another one of my notes?

sources.text: Focus On One Thing: Do one thing. Do it well. Do it for a long time. That is how to become skilled and successful.
Focus On One Thing: Your destination is a huge mountain peak on the horizon. You can see it from everywhere. Yes to that mountain, and no to everything else.
Embodiment: Mental patients were asked to fill in a personality test acting as if they were a "typical, well-adjusted person".
Focus On One Thing: Any business model works. It's not the model, it's the person behind the model that determines success.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Somewhere an advert promises the one trick that changes your whole working life. Before the jingle ends, you've opened a tab.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ah, the eager man of new ideas. Every morning a fresh opportunity lands on the step like the milk, and a sensible soul seizes it before the wind changes. Find the right door and run through it at once.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's the comfortable lie, isn't it? Jump on the good one fast and you win.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Don't you dare agree with it yet. I agree with nothing before I've read it, March.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Charming's not a plan.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Cruel, and accurate.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then hear the thing itself. The note says: “Do one thing. Do it well. Do it for a long time. That is how to become skilled and successful.” Commands stacked on the table, and no room left for the shiny thing.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the trick isn't a trick. It's sticking with one thing long enough to get decent at it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You've said it plainer than I would, which is an insult I shall forgive.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Test it. Say someone keeps a notebook on the windowsill with a new business model on every page, and each one is dead by the end of the week. Count the pages out loud, narrator. One per turn.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: One.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Go on.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: One. And another, and one more after that...

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's not a count, that's a sigh with ink on it. Keep going.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I decline to say the total aloud. It is embarrassing, March, and I am far too well bred.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Every page got a bright start and a quiet ending. Nobody stayed long enough to find out what the model could do.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The model was never the trouble. The note is quite clear: “Any business model works.” Then the person behind it decides.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the page isn't the problem. The person holding the pen is.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now look out of that window, the very one you're standing at. Yonder, the hill. A mountain, March, the note's own mountain.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: “Your destination is a huge mountain peak on the horizon. You can see it from everywhere. Yes to that mountain, and no to everything else.”

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Any hill with a radio mast on it, narrator, was there before the note. The hill didn't read the note.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the mast is a sign. Sent to whoever happens to be looking, and I, ever the looker, am looking.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You're being very unbearable.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Thank you, I try.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I'll give you the hard part, since you're so keen on plain truths. A sign is only a sign if you stay put long enough to see it again. Most people see it once, from a moving car, and call it destiny. Then they drive on...

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: ...and the hill goes unvisited for years. There's the storyteller admitting the hill is a hill. Write that down.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I am writing nothing. It's late and I am tired of biros.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Bring in the other note, the embodiment one. “Mental patients were asked to fill in a personality test acting as if they were a “typical, well-adjusted person”.” Then they started feeling it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the acting turned into feeling. Pretend long enough, March, and the feeling trots along behind you like a dog that was never called.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the mountain's not a task list. It's who you've got to be to keep walking at it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The identity walks. The calendar merely keeps the record of the walk.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Here's where they cross. Focus without the embodiment is willpower, gone by Thursday.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Embodiment without focus is pretending. A well-adjusted person who never finishes a single thing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Both notes, and one crossing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The mountain needs a walker, and the walker needs a mountain, or he is merely a fellow exercising in a field.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Neither note shows that alone. Focus by itself is willpower. Embodiment by itself is a costume.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A costume with a mountain painted on the back of it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Showing off again.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Someone who believes this keeps one project on the shelf. Every new offer gets one question: does it move me toward the mountain, or away? They say no far more often than they expect to. Each no comes easier, because by then they've started to look like the one who stays.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You've built a whole fork out of a shelf, March. I am impressed.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Just take the compliment, narrator.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I'll take it, and I'll stop complaining about the stool. Mostly.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Mostly's a start. And don't ask me the score, because I keep it to myself.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I wouldn't dream of asking. I shall simply note that you keep one, the way a dog keeps a bone.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then here is my pick for the one thing, March. The tin. The open one on the windowsill, and I shall stay devoted to it until I'm grey.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The tin was the one thing all along, narrator. You just had to stop calling it a kingdom.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A kingdom reduced to a biscuit tin. I am wounded, and devoted.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You keep Warden of the Open Tin. Keeper stays with the hinge oiler.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the stool and I are reconciled, for tonight.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's gone past midnight, so put the kettle on and bring the tin. Up next, the other half of these notes: the one about becoming the person before the picture arrives.
